stages.name: State provision of public goods
stages.title: State provision of public goods
stages.sub: What happens when the government, rather than the market, provides a public good.

steps.q: Every passing ship benefits from a lighthouse whether it paid or not. Could a private firm easily charge each ship?
steps.right: No, it could not charge people individually
steps.wrong: Yes, it could charge each ship separately
steps.hint: Think about whether anyone can be stopped from using the light, or whether one ship's use uses it up.

steps.q: Once the government builds the lighthouse from taxes, can any ship still use its light without paying extra?
steps.right: Yes, but everyone has already paid through tax
steps.wrong: No, ships must still pay per use
steps.hint: Nobody can dodge the tax that funds it the way they could dodge a private charge.

steps.q: If a private firm ran the lighthouse and could charge, would poorer ship owners who couldn't afford it still get protection?
steps.right: No, they would be left without it
steps.wrong: Yes, price would not affect who gets it
steps.hint: A market price always excludes whoever cannot pay it. Does state funding do that?
steps.pre: Because it is paid for by everyone's taxes, government provision instead

steps.q: A private firm reads demand from the prices people will pay. When the government provides a public good free, does it get that signal?
steps.right: No, it has no price signal to guide it
steps.wrong: Yes, it can see exactly what people want
steps.hint: Without asymmetric-information-style feedback from prices, how does the state know if it is building two lighthouses or twenty?

steps.right: No, there is less pressure to keep costs down
steps.wrong: Yes, the pressure is exactly the same
